description: 2nd-year Astronomy & Space Sciences student at Istanbul University with experience in observational astronomy and Ul design. Building an interactive citizen-science web tool (blink comparator & IR band filter) for NASA SPHEREx. Currently working solo.
summary: NYXE is a browser-based console built for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge that lets anyone explore real SPHEREx-era sky data the way a citizen scientist would. It fetches real IRSA/SPHEREx image cutouts and cross-matches them against SIMBAD and SkyBoT, then overlays spectral, proper-motion and brightness information across four observing epochs so users can spot moving, color-changing or variable objects — inspired by tools like WiseView. A synthetic “Discovery Map” mode offers the same workflow with a procedurally generated sky, so anyone can practice the discovery process even without a live connection. Found candidates can be saved with an automatic category suggestion (brown dwarf, variable, moving object, etc.) driven by SIMBAD type, proper motion and a Planck spectral fit. The app supports five languages, exports analysis-ready data via Python, and degrades gracefully when NASA/IPAC or CDS services are briefly unavailable — something we ran into often while building and testing it.
details:
What it does & how it works

NYXE is a browser-based console for exploring SPHEREx-era time-domain sky data the way a citizen scientist would. Users can pick a real target (e.g. Barnard’s Star, ε Indi Ba/Bb, WISE 0855−0714) or any coordinate, and the app fetches real SPHEREx pixel cutouts and catalog data from NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive via its TAP service, cross-matches the field against SIMBAD for object identity, type, proper motion and parallax, and against IMCCE’s SkyBoT for known Solar System bodies. The app overlays this across four observing epochs (Jan 2025 – Jul 2026) so a user can blink, diff, or scrub between dates and spot objects that moved, brightened, dimmed, or changed color — the same kind of visual search that let WiseView volunteers find real brown dwarfs in WISE data. A built-in diagnostic engine (motion detection, pair-wise brightness comparison, and a Planck blackbody fit to the SPHEREx spectrum) automatically suggests what kind of object a candidate might be (moving object, variable, brown-dwarf-like, etc.), while still letting the user override the category themselves before saving it. A separate “Discovery Map” mode reproduces the same workflow over a procedurally generated synthetic sky, so the discovery process stays usable for teaching or demos even without a live connection.

Benefits & intended impact

SPHEREx is producing a 102-band, all-sky spectral map, and (like WISE before it) this kind of dataset has historically rewarded public, visual inspection — not just automated pipelines. NYXE lowers the barrier to doing that: no account, no download, no coding knowledge required, just a browser. It is aimed at students, astronomy clubs, and citizen-science volunteers who want a genuine, if simplified, entry point into real SPHEREx data and the kind of time-domain reasoning (motion, variability, color change) that underlies discoveries like new brown dwarfs, nearby variable stars, or — in the spirit of the challenge — unusual outer-solar-system objects.

Tools, languages & services used

The app is a single-page React application (no build framework dependency at runtime — bundled with esbuild and a custom Tailwind-based style layer), deployed as a static site on GitHub Pages. It talks directly to NASA/IPAC IRSA’s TAP service for SPHEREx cutouts/catalogs, CDS’s SIMBAD TAP service for object cross-matching, IMCCE’s SkyBoT for moving-object ephemerides, and CDS’s hips2fits service (2MASS/AllWISE) for reference sky imagery. It supports five UI languages (Turkish, English, Spanish, German, Japanese) and includes a Python-export feature so a user can continue analysis of a saved candidate locally (e.g. in a Jupyter notebook) with the exact FITS/TAP query that produced it.

Creativity & design factors

The main design challenge was making a real, messy NASA archive feel approachable without hiding how uncertain real data can be. Rather than only showing a “success” state, NYXE is built around graceful, honest degradation: when IRSA, SIMBAD or the imaging service are slow, blocked by CORS, or briefly down (which happened repeatedly during development — including on submission day), the app says so plainly, offers a retry, and falls back to the synthetic engine or a locally uploaded FITS file instead of silently failing or showing fabricated data. Every automatically suggested object category is labeled with why it was suggested (SIMBAD type, a measured spectrum fit, a flux change between epochs, or detected motion) so the reasoning stays visible and the user — not the algorithm — makes the final call.

Use of AI assistance (disclosure)

Code for this project was written with the assistance of an AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), used interactively throughout development for implementation, debugging, and test-writing; all data, scientific logic, and design decisions were directed and reviewed by the team. No NASA branding, logos, or mission identifiers were used or generated. No AI-generated images, video, or audio are included in the project.
